info.title: Map backend and shared systems (@explore subagent)

parts.text:
I'm building a wiki for the repository at /tmp/openwiki-bench-pS6clC (a Cloudflare Workers-based "Gadgets Workshop" platform). I need a thorough understanding of the backend and shared RPC layer. Be "very thorough".

Read and summarize:
1. packages/workshop-shared/src/api.ts — the RPC API. Note its major interfaces (AuthenticatedApi, workspace/gadget/chat/auth methods), limits.ts, code-change.ts, gatekeeper.ts, external-message-gateway.ts, feature-flags.ts, theme.ts, cloudflare-gatekeeper.ts.
2. packages/workshop-backend/src — key systems:
   - server.ts (entrypoint, routing, websocket)
   - user.ts (user DO, gatekeeper class enforcement, AuthContext)
   - overseer.ts (chat/agent orchestration, prepareChatBindings)
   - agent.ts, agent-catalog.ts
   - admin-config.ts, admin-settings.ts (AdminConfig, AdminSettings DO)
   - provisioning-policy.ts
   - sharing.ts, access.ts
   - ai-models.ts, ai-invoke.ts, ai-gateway.ts, ai-gateway-billing/
   - auth/ (auth-vendors, config, login-flow)
   - observability.ts
   - slash-commands.ts
   - blueprint-archive.ts, gadget-export.ts, format-blueprints.ts, browser-export.ts
   - external-message-gateway.ts, web-fetch.ts, do-retry.ts
   - client-errors.ts, code-preview.ts, deployment-config.ts, export-limits.ts, feature-flags.ts, git-store.ts, git-migration.ts, analytics.ts
3. packages/router (entrypoint, routing)
4. packages/typed-storage
5. packages/backend-utils

For each system report: purpose, key files/classes with their responsibilities, data flow, persistence (Durable Objects, KV), auth/security, invariants, failure handling, and how the parts connect.

Report back a structured summary with concrete file paths and line numbers.
I'll thoroughly explore the repository's backend and shared RPC layer. Let me start by getting an overview of the structure and then dive deep into each system.

parts.text: This is a large codebase. Let me read the key files systematically. Let me start with the shared API.

state.output:
<path>/tmp/openwiki-bench-pS6clC/packages/workshop-shared/src/api.ts</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: // This file defines the API spoken between the Gadgets Workshop service and the front-end UI.
2: //
3: // The UI is a good old "fat client" SPA. Why not use SSR? Because:
4: // - Users of this UI are likely to have it open often, maybe even all the time. Startup time is
5: //   less of a concern than with sites you visit only briefly, and assets are likely to be in cache
6: //   in any case.
7: // - The Gadgets themselves are sandboxed on the client side in addition to the server side. This
8: //   sandboxing requires running code in the browser. It is not plausible to server-side render
9: //   a Gadget itself.
10: // - By providing a really clean API boundary between client and server, we make it easier to build
11: //   alternative clients.
12: // - SPA is just easier to think about.
13: //
14: // The entire API between the client and server is an RPC API, using Cloudflare's JavaScript RPC,
15: // which essentially allows natural JavaScript / TypeScript interfaces to be exposed over the
16: // network.
17: //
18: // The RPC interface operates over a WebSocket, which the client starts immediately at startup and
19: // keeps open for the entire lifetime of the session, reconnecting if needed.
20: //
21: // Gadgets run inside a sandboxed iframe which has no ability to talk to the outside world at all,
22: // except postMessage() to the parent frame. Through postMessage() exchanges, the Gadget can speak
23: // RPC to the Workshop. Among other things, through this interface, the Workshop provides the
24: // Gadget a stub pointing to the Gadget's server-side Durable Object interface.
25: 
26: import { RpcCompatible, RpcStub, RpcTarget } from "capnweb";
27: import { AccountDescription, ActionKind, ActionDescription, AvatarImage, GatekeeperUiFrame, ObservationDescription, ResourceDescription, ResourceConfiguratorFrame, SupportedResource, VendorDescription, HookDescription } from "./gatekeeper.js";
28: import type { CodeChange } from "./code-change.js";
29: import type { UiFeatureFlags } from "./feature-flags.js";
30: 
31: export const SERVICE_SALT = new Uint8Array([
32:   0xd9, 0x4e, 0x54, 0x1d, 0x29, 0xc1, 0x03, 0x74, 0x73, 0x7e, 0xb3, 0xe3, 0x34, 0x6d, 0x8f, 0x21
33: ]);
34: 
35: /**
36:  * A pending gatekeeper sign-in attempt, returned by `PublicApi.startGatekeeperLogin()`. Holding this
37:  * stub is the capability to receive the resulting session token; dispose it to abandon the attempt.
38:  */
39: export interface LoginAttempt extends RpcTarget {
40:   /**
41:    * Resolves with a session token (to store and pass to `authenticate()`, same format as `login()`)
42:    * once the gatekeeper popup completes, or rejects if the attempt fails or is abandoned. Safe to
43:    * call immediately after `startGatekeeperLogin()`.
44:    */
45:   wait(): Promise<string>;
46: }
47: 
48: /** Public API exposed to the internet. */
49: export interface PublicApi extends RpcTarget {
50:   /** Confirms that the RPC connection can round-trip without performing application work. */
51:   ping(): Promise<void>;
52: 
53:   /**
54:    * Returns deployment-level configuration the client needs at boot (auth mode, available sign-in
55:    * vendors, whether the Cloudflare limits flow is enabled). Contains no secrets.
56:    */
57:   getServerConfig(): Promise<ServerConfig>;
58: 
59:   /**
60:    * Begin a sign-in via an authentication gatekeeper (e.g. "google", "github", "cloudflare").
61:    * Returns a `url` the client opens in a new tab (the gatekeeper's OAuth popup, which self-closes)
62:    * and an `attempt` stub whose `wait()` resolves once the popup completes. The vendor must be
63:    * auth-capable and allowlisted (see ServerConfig.authVendors); throws otherwise.
64:    *
65:    * Dispose `attempt` to abandon the sign-in (e.g. the user closed the popup); this cancels the wait
66:    * server-side.
67:    */
68:   startGatekeeperLogin(vendorId: string): Promise<{ url: string; attempt: RpcStub<LoginAttempt> }>;
69: 
70:   /** Authenticates the user using an auth token (typically stored in localStorage). */
71:   authenticate(token: string): Promise<AuthenticatedApi>;
72: 
73:   /**
74:    * Like authenticate() but the server is expected to be sitting behind Cloudflare Access, and the
75:    * client is expected to have already authenticated with Access (before they could load the
76:    * application in their browser at all). The credentials from the Cloudflare Access session will
77:    * be used to authenticate the user.
78:    */
79:   authenticateFromCfAccess(): Promise<AuthenticatedApi>;
80: 
81:   /**
82:    * Login with username and password.
83:    *
84:    * Returns a token to store in local storage and pass to `authenticate()` in the future.
85:    *
86:    * Returns null if login failed (no such user or wrong password).
87:    *
88:    * `passwordHash` is derived from the user's password as follows:
89:    *
90:    *     argon2id({
91:    *       password,
92:    *       salt: SERVICE_SALT + encode(username, 'utf8'),
93:    *       parallelism: 1,
94:    *       iterations: 3,
95:    *       memorySize: 64MiB,
96:    *       hashLength: 32,
97:    *     });
98:    *
99:    * Note that the `passwordHash` itself is NOT stored plaintext by the server -- additional
100:    * hashing is performed server-side. The overall scheme achieves roughly the same security
101:    * guarantees as traditional server-side password hashing, but with the added benefit that the
102:    * server never sees the user's password at all, and also the benefit of performing the expensive
103:    * hash on the client which tends to have more resources available than a busy server.
104:    *
105:    * This API may be disabled when the server uses SSO for authentication.
106:    */
107:   login(username: string, passwordHash: Uint8Array): Promise<string | null>;
108: 
109:   /**
110:    * Create a new account. Returns a token to store in local storage and pass to `authenticate()`
111:    * in the future.
112:    *
113:    * Returns null if the username already exists. (Other kinds of errors may throw exceptions.)
114:    *
115:    * See login() (above) for an explanation of the password hashing algorithm.
116:    *
117:    * This API may be disabled when the server uses SSO for authentication.
118:    */
119:   createAccount(username: string, displayName: string, passwordHash: Uint8Array)
120:       : Promise<string | null>;
121: 
122:   /**
123:    * Fetch blueprint metadata by ID. Returns null if the blueprint doesn't exist. No
124:    * authentication required (knowing the ID is sufficient, since a blueprint is "just data").
125:    */
126:   getBlueprint(id: string): Promise<BlueprintPublicInfo | null>;
127: 
128:   /**
129:    * Download a blueprint as a `.gadget` archive stream. The archive contains only
130:    * BlueprintMetadata plus the current blueprint code snapshot, not the full KV record.
131:    */
132:   downloadBlueprint(id: string): Promise<ReadableStream<Uint8Array>>;
133: }
134: 
135: /** Subscription callback for AuthenticatedApi.subscribeConnectedAccounts(). */
136: export interface ConnectedAccountsSubscriber {
137:   /**
138:    * If `credentialsValid` is false, the account's credentials are known to be expired, and the
139:    * UI should call reconnectAccount() to fix this if the user tries to select this account.
140:    */
141:   add(id: number, description: AccountDescription, vendor: VendorDescription,
142:       supportedResources: SupportedResource[], credentialsValid: boolean, vendorId: string): void;
143:   remove(id: number): void;
144: 
145:   /** Called after add() has been called for all accounts known so far. */
146:   ready(): void;
147: }
148: 
149: /**
150:  * When listing gatekeeper vendors or connected accounts, you can filter to only vendors/accounts
151:  * that support certain features. This type specifies the filter.
152:  */
153: export type GatekeeperVendorFilter = {
154:   /** Filter for vendors that can connect to the given resource. */
155:   resourceUrl?: string,
156: };

164: /**
165:  * Identifies a workpiece within a workspace. A workpiece is a numbered thing the user (or agent)
166:  * is working on inside the workspace -- currently a gadget or a gatekeeper (connection), with
167:  * more types expected later. All workpiece types share one sequential per-workspace ID namespace,
168:  * so a bare number unambiguously identifies a workpiece of any type, and derived names (facet
169:  * names) can never collide across types.
170:  */
171: export type WorkpieceId = number;
172: 
173: // Matches an ASCII JavaScript identifier, excluding `$`. Deliberately conservative: binding
174: // names are typed by agents and rendered as `env.NAME`, so full Unicode identifier support buys
175: // nothing; and while `$` is technically legal in identifiers, it is conventionally reserved for
176: // special circumstances like code generators, so agents shouldn't be using it.
177: const IDENTIFIER_REGEX = /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/;
178: 
179: // ECMAScript reserved words (including strict-mode reservations and literals), which are valid
180: // per IDENTIFIER_REGEX but cannot follow `.` in all contexts and would confuse both agents and
181: // humans as binding names.
182: const RESERVED_WORDS = new Set([
183:   "break", "case", "catch", "class", "const", "continue", "debugger", "default", "delete", "do",
184:   "else", "enum", "export", "extends", "false", "finally", "for", "function", "if", "import",
185:   "in", "instanceof", "new", "null", "return", "super", "switch", "this", "throw", "true", "try",
186:   "typeof", "var", "void", "while", "with",
187:   // Strict-mode / contextual reservations.
188:   "await", "implements", "interface", "let", "package", "private", "protected", "public",
189:   "static", "yield",
190: ]);
191: 
192: /**
193:  * Validates a binding name, throwing a descriptive Error if it is unacceptable. This is the one
194:  * shared validator applied at every chokepoint that writes a binding name (gadget binding edges,
195:  * the workspace default binding list, chat binding maps, spawner env configs, and the agent
196:  * tools), wherever the map is keyed.
197:  *
198:  * A valid name is a JavaScript identifier (see IDENTIFIER_REGEX; reserved words excluded) that is
199:  * not a dangerous or confusing property name: anything that exists on `Object.prototype`
200:  * (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `toString`, etc.) or `prototype` is rejected,
201:  * since binding maps are used as plain objects where such names would collide with inherited
202:  * members -- or worse, mutate the prototype chain.
203:  *
204:  * ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES is style guidance only (recommended in tool descriptions and used by
205:  * generated names), not enforced here.
206:  */
207: export function validateBindingName(name: string): void {
208:   if (!IDENTIFIER_REGEX.test(name)) {
209:     throw new Error(
210:         `Invalid binding name "${name}": binding names must be JavaScript identifiers ` +
211:         `(letters, digits, and '_', not starting with a digit).`);
212:   }
213:   if (RESERVED_WORDS.has(name)) {
214:     throw new Error(`Invalid binding name "${name}": this is a reserved word in JavaScript.`);
215:   }
216:   if (name === "prototype" || name in Object.prototype) {
217:     throw new Error(
218:         `Invalid binding name "${name}": this name collides with a built-in object property.`);
219:   }
220: }

222: /**
223:  * Why a previously-configured observer binding failed verification on this open attempt. Attached to
224:  * the ObserverBindingNeed the overseer re-prompts with, so the client can explain what went wrong
225:  * instead of dead-ending the open.
226:  */
227: export type ObserverBindingFailure = {
228:   /**
229:    * The account that was tried and rejected (a ConnectedAccountRecord id in the opening user's own
230:    * User DO). Re-authenticating it in place is usually the fix, so the client should pre-select it
231:    * and aim its re-authenticate affordance at it. May no longer exist, if the user disconnected it.
232:    */
233:   accountId: number;
234:   /**
235:    * Human-readable explanation for display: either the error the gatekeeper threw when it refused
236:    * the account, or a message the overseer authored itself for a cause it can see directly (e.g.
237:    * the chosen account is no longer connected). Free text: MUST NOT be parsed or matched on.
238:    */
239:   reason: string;
240: };
241: 
242: /**
243:  * Describes one connection a non-owner must verify using one of their own accounts. Passed to
244:  * ObserverConfigCallback.configure() when the opening user needs to choose an account; its result
245:  * echoes `gatekeeperId` in an ObserverAccountChoice.
246:  */
247: export type ObserverBindingNeed = {
248:   /** The overseer-assigned gatekeeper id (a workpiece id). */
249:   gatekeeperId: WorkpieceId;
250:   /**
251:    * The vendor the user must have a connected account for (e.g. "google"). The frontend filters
252:    * the user's connected accounts by this to find candidates.
253:    */
254:   vendorId: string;
255:   /** Human-readable resource title, for display in the configuration modal. */
256:   resourceTitle: string;
257:   /** Canonical resource URL, if known, for display. */
258:   resourceUrl?: string;
259:   /**
260:    * Set only when this binding was already configured but its chosen account failed verification on
261:    * this attempt (expired credentials, a revoked grant, an upstream outage, or a genuine denial).
262:    * Absent for a binding that has simply never been configured. Deliberately carries no
263:    * "credentials valid" flag: the client already has that live from subscribeConnectedAccounts, and
264:    * a copy on the wire would go stale while the modal is open across an OAuth round trip.
265:    */
266:   failure?: ObserverBindingFailure;
267: };

269: /**
270:  * The opening user's chosen account for a single gatekeeper binding. Returned from
271:  * ObserverConfigCallback.configure().
272:  */
273: export type ObserverAccountChoice = {
274:   /** Matches the ObserverBindingNeed.gatekeeperId being satisfied. */
275:   gatekeeperId: WorkpieceId;
276:   /** An account in the opening user's own User DO (a ConnectedAccountRecord id). */
277:   accountId: number;
278: };

280: /**
281:  * Provided by the client when opening a gadget. Invoked by the overseer ONLY if the opening user
282:  * must choose connected accounts for one or more gatekeeper bindings before they can observe the
283:  * gadget. In the common case (owner, or an already-configured observer) this is never called and
284:  * open() resolves without an extra round trip. The overseer does not resolve open() until this
285:  * returns. If the user cannot or will not provide the needed accounts, the callback should reject,
286:  * and the overseer denies the open.
287:  *
288:  * `configure()` may be called a second time within one open, for the subset of bindings that failed
289:  * verification (each carrying an ObserverBindingNeed.failure). This lets the user repair a binding --
290:  * typically by re-authenticating the account whose credentials expired -- without leaving the flow.
291:  * The overseer bounds the number of such re-prompts, so a client that resubmits an account that
292:  * keeps failing eventually gets a denial rather than an endless loop.
293:  */
294: export interface ObserverConfigCallback extends RpcTarget {
295:   configure(needs: ObserverBindingNeed[]): Promise<ObserverAccountChoice[]>;
296: }

298: /** Builds the create/read helpers for a family of expected errors carrying stable
299:  * machine-readable codes. The per-code messages double as the classification fallback for errors
300:  * from older deployments that lost the code in transit, so changing one is a compatibility break. */
301: function codedErrorFamily<Code extends string>(messages: Record<Code, string>) {
302:   const codes = new Set<unknown>(Object.keys(messages));
303:   return {
304:     create: (code: Code): Error & { code: Code } =>
305:         Object.assign(new Error(messages[code]), { code }),
306:     getCode: (error: unknown): Code | undefined => {
307:       const candidate = typeof error === "object" && error !== null && "code" in error
308:           ? error.code : undefined;
309:       return codes.has(candidate) ? candidate as Code : undefined;
310:     },
311:   };
312: }

324: const openGadgetErrors = codedErrorFamily<OpenGadgetErrorCode>({
325:   [OPEN_GADGET_ERROR_CODES.workspaceNotFound]: "Workspace not found.",

335: /** Stable error codes attached to authentication failures. */

344: /** Messages for auth failures thrown without a surviving code; clients match these only as a

1598:   /**
1599:    * Get metadata describing this workspace and subscribe to changes.

1602:    * changes.

1604:    * Disposing the returned `RpcStub` will cancel the subscription.

1608:       : Promise<RpcStub<{}>>;

1610:   /**
1611:    * Receive the current viewer roster, then incremental updates as viewers come and go.
1612:    * A viewer is present for the lifetime of the openGadget() session.
1613:    */
1614:   subscribeToPresence(subscriber: RpcStub<PresenceSubscriber>): Promise<RpcStub<{}>>;
1615: 
1616:   /** Change the workspace title. */
1617:   setTitle(title: string): Promise<void>;
1618: 
1619:   /** Pin or unpin this workspace in the user's list. */
1620:   setPinned(pinned: boolean): Promise<void>;
1621: 
1622:   /**
1623:    * Instruct the workspace to delete itself, removing it from the User's workspace list and
1624:    * deleting all data. Further method calls will fail.
1625:    *
1626:    * TODO: Implement undelete, maybe using PITR...
1627:    */
1628:   deleteSelf(): Promise<void>;
1629: 
1630:   /**
1631:    * Subscribe to the workspace's workpiece list.
1632:    *
1633:    * The subscriber receives one entry() per existing workpiece, followed by ready(), then
1634:    * incremental entry()/removed() calls as workpieces are created, renamed, or deleted. In v1

1636:    *

1647:    * `createdGadgets`), and the gadget remains pending (see WorkpieceSummary.chatId) until
1648:    * the user accepts the chat's changes through that message (merging deletes the pending marker;
1649:    * reverting deletes the gadget). Without `chatId` the gadget is created permanently, with an
1650:    * empty initial commit as its head (see WorkpieceSummary.commitId).

1652:    * `bindingName` is the name under which the gadget appears in chat envs and the workspace
1653:    * default binding list (see validateBindingName()). When absent, the server chooses one from

1668:   /**
1669:    * Read the full contents of a commit in the workspace's git object store: one
1670:    * `[path, content]` entry per file, with nested trees flattened to `/`-joined paths. Paths are
1671:    * unique; entry order carries no meaning. (`files` is a list of pairs rather than a path-keyed
1672:    * object so that file names like `__proto__`, which RPC deserialization drops from object
1673:    * keys, survive in transit -- see CodeChange in `@gadgets/workshop-shared/code-change`.)
1674:    *
1675:    * Commits are immutable, so responses are cacheable client-side by commit ID. Use this to view
1676:    * committed code (outside any chat, or for a gadget the open chat has no pin for) and to fetch
1677:    * the base content of a chat's pins (see ChatCodeBase).
1678:    */
1679:   getCodeAtCommit(commitId: string): Promise<{files: [path: string, content: string][]}>;

1681:   /**
1682:    * Walk the commit graph from `fromCommit` (that commit first, then its ancestry), returning up
1683:    * to `depth` commits' metadata -- all reachable commits when `depth` is omitted. Traversal
1684:    * order for merge commits follows git log's default (reverse chronological). Like
1685:    * getCodeAtCommit(), results are immutable and cacheable.
1686:    */
1687:   getCommitLog(fromCommit: string, depth?: number): Promise<CommitInfo[]>;
1688: 
1689:   /**
1690:    * Submit one code change on a chat's branch. This is the only way to edit code: committed code
1691:    * cannot be written directly -- gadget heads only advance when a chat's changes are accepted
1692:    * (see mergeChanges()).
1693:    *
1694:    * `submission.change` is expressed against the chat's content as of
1695:    * `(submission.generation, submission.revision)` -- that is, the submitter has applied every
1696:    * accepted change of that generation's stream up to and including that revision (see
1697:    * ChatCodeBase). The server transforms the change over any changes accepted since, validates it,
1698:    * appends it to the stream, and broadcasts it (AiChatSubscriber.changeApplied()); the returned
1699:    * `(generation, revision)` is where it landed.
1700:    *
1701:    * `submission.pins` must carry one declaration per *permanent* gadget the change touches that is
1702:    * not yet pinned in the chat, each naming the head commit the client's content derives from.
1703:    * The server checks that each declared base is the gadget's current head, or a parent of it
1704:    * (tolerating a race with one concurrent merge), and establishes the pin atomically with the
1705:    * change. A declaration identical to the existing pin is accepted idempotently; one naming a
1706:    * different `baseCommit` (a race between two first editors) throws. Exception: a gadget still
1707:    * pending in this chat has no head commit to pin (see WorkpieceSummary.commitId), so its changes
1708:    * carry no declaration and build its content up from nothing (see ChatCodeBase).
1709:    *
1710:    * Retries: `submission.clientId` names the client's editing session and `submission.seq`
1711:    * numbers its submissions from 1. The server remembers each session's last accepted seq and
1712:    * where it landed -- independently of the changes themselves, so recognition survives
1713:    * materialization, epoch resets, and destructive generation bumps -- and answers a retry of
1714:    * that seq with the recorded result instead of applying it twice. A transport failure must
1715:    * therefore be retried with the *same* seq and an identical payload, never renumbered or
1716:    * re-composed (OT, unlike a CRDT, does not tolerate double-application); a same-seq
1717:    * submission whose content differs is a client bug and is rejected. A seq one past the last
1718:    * accepted (or 1 from a new session) is the next change; anything else is rejected -- discard
1719:    * local edits and rebuild under a fresh clientId. Only the last submission is remembered, so
1720:    * keep at most one in flight.
1721:    *
1722:    * While an agent turn is active, the call throws a retryable error: keep the queued change and
1723:    * resubmit after the turn ends. (The UI already locks editing during turns; this backstops
1724:    * races.)
1725:    *
1726:    * A submission still rooted in the *previous* generation, when that generation was closed by
1727:    * a merge (a content-preserving bump; see ChatCodeBase.generation), is transformed across the
1728:    * boundary and lands in the current generation, so typing straight through someone's accept
1729:    * is seamless. Such a submission's pin declarations are ignored (they describe pre-merge
1730:    * heads; the server derives the new pins itself), and it is rejected if it touches a gadget
1731:    * in ChatCodeBase.prior.discontinuousGadgets (the merge visibly changed that gadget's
1732:    * content) or a gadget that has since been re-pinned at a different base.
1733:    *
1734:    * Every other rejection means the client's local state is unusable: a generation ended by a
1735:    * destructive bump (revert, draft discard, turn abort), a revision older than the server's
1736:    * retained transform window, or an invalid change all mean the client must discard its local
1737:    * edits and rebuild from fresh metadata.
1738:    */
1739:   submitCodeChange(chatId: number, submission: CodeChangeSubmission)
1740:       : Promise<{generation: number, revision: number}>;

2274: /**

2278:  * changes fast-forwards each touched gadget's head (see Overseer.mergeChanges()). A gadget
2279:  * joins the stream only when its code is first *modified* in the chat -- at that moment it is
2280:  * pinned at a commit, whose tree its changes apply on top of. Unpinned gadgets always track
2281:  * mainline head, live, and are read via Overseer.getCodeAtCommit(). One exception: a gadget

2284:  * that makes it permanent ends the epoch anyway, and in later epochs it pins like any other

2288:  * (Overseer.getCodeAtCommit(baseCommit)); apply the current epoch's non-reverted `changes`

2297:   /**

2301:    * but the content carries over -- `prior` describes the closed stream, and in-flight
2302:    * submissions are transformed onto the new generation (see submitCodeChange()). **Destructive**

2304:    * clients may have transformed against is gone, so they must discard local state and rebuild.

2307:   generation: number;
2308: 
2309:   /**

2311:    * message, or a migrated chat's `conversionBoundary` changes message. Absent when the epoch

2313:    * chat's current content.

2317:   /**

2319:    * numbered sequentially from 1; 0 means none yet). Restarts with each generation, so

2321:    * field is a snapshot as of this metadata delivery; clients track the live position via
2322:    * AiChatSubscriber.changeApplied().
2323:    */
2324:   revision: number;

2326:   /**

2328:    * closed generation so clients can hand off to the new one without losing anything. A client
2329:    * still processing generation `prior.generation` first applies its remaining changeApplied()
2330:    * deliveries -- that stream is complete once seen through `finalRevision` -- and then
2331:    * switches. Content is identical across the boundary for every gadget except those listed in
2332:    * `discontinuousGadgets`, which must be rebuilt from head (dropping pending local changes that

2334:    * closed stream is unusable anyway.

2337:     /** The closed generation. */
2338:     generation: number;

2340:     /** The closed generation's terminal revision: its stream is complete through here. */

2343:     /**

2352: /**

2355:  * changes apply on top of. A pin is established by that first modification -- a
2356:  * submitCodeChange() pin declaration, or the agent's first write, which pins at the then-current

3320:    * call's delta stream), but a preview outlives its streaming: tool calls execute only after
3321:    * the whole model response has streamed, so several previews can finish before any of their
3322:    * durable rows exists. The client must keep displaying each finished preview's final text --
3323:    * a call's edits would otherwise vanish until its row lands -- until the preview resolves,
3324:    * which happens in one of two ways: the completed call's change row arrives via
3325:    * AiChatSubscriber.changeApplied() carrying the same final content (the ordinary end), or an
3326:    * editPreviewClear withdraws it because no row will come. Since rows arrive in call order,
3327:    * per-file previews resolve oldest-first. As with all provisional state, the client should
3328:    * also discard whatever remains when the agent stops running.
3329:    */
3330:   type: "editPreviewStart";
3331:   toolCallId: string;
3332:   file: { workpieceId: WorkpieceId, filename: string };
3333:   /**
3334:    * For editFile: the exact text being replaced. The client finds its unique match in the file
3335:    * (skipping the preview if there isn't exactly one -- the call itself will then fail). Absent
3336:    * for writeFile, whose streamed content replaces the whole file.
3337:    */
3338:   textToReplace?: string;
3339: } | {
3340:   /** Appends newly decoded characters to the streaming edit preview's content. */
3341:   type: "editPreviewDelta";
3342:   toolCallId: string;
3343:   delta: string;
3344: } | {
3345:   /**
3346:    * Withdraws an edit preview whose tool call will produce no change row -- its input failed to
3347:    * parse or validate, the call failed, or the edit turned out to be a no-op. May name any call
3348:    * of the current response, not just the one currently streaming (failures surface at
3349:    * execution, after later calls' previews may have started). The client restores the previewed
3350:    * file to its real content. (Successful calls emit no clear: the durable changeApplied row
3351:    * supersedes the preview instead.)
3352:    */
3353:   type: "editPreviewClear";
3354:   toolCallId: string;
3355: } | {
3356:   /**
3357:    * Streaming createGadget output format, used by the UI before the finalized tool call arrives.
3358:    * Has the deployment's overrides applied, so it matches what the gadget is stamped with.
3359:    */
3360:   type: "toolCallOutputFormat";
3361:   toolCallId: string;
3362:   output: BlueprintOutput;
3363: } | {
3364:   type: "toolOutputDelta";
3365:   toolCallId: string;
3366:   delta: string;
3367: };

3389:    * opaque value identifying the current server (Overseer DO) instance. If a resubscribing client
3390:    * sees a different value than on its previous subscription, the DO has fully restarted since
3391:    * then, meaning any in-flight provisional stream content was lost and will be re-streamed from
3392:    * scratch; the client should discard its provisional streaming state. An unchanged value (a
3393:    * plain network reconnect to the same live instance) means provisional state should be kept.
3394:    */
3395:   streamGeneration(generation: number): void;
3396: 
3397:   /** Metadata for the given chat thread has changed, or a new chat thread was created. */
3398:   metadata(chat: AiChatMetadata): void;
3399: 
3400:   /** Indicates the chat thread was deleted. */
3401:   deleted(chatId: number): void;
3402: 
3403:   /** Adds a message to the chat. */
3404:   message(msg: AiChatMessage): void;
3405: 
3406:   /**
3407:    * Delivers one accepted change of a chat's change stream: a human submitCodeChange(), an agent
3408:    * tool edit (broadcast when the tool call completes, superseding the provisional editPreview*
3409:    * stream of its in-progress content -- see AiChatStreamEvent), or an updateChatFromMainline()
3410:    * merge. Changes must be applied in
3411:    * revision order within a generation; a gap means events were lost and the client should
3412:    * rebuild from fresh metadata and history. On a generation switch, first finish the old
3413:    * generation's remaining changes -- complete once seen through
3414:    * ChatCodeBase.prior.finalRevision -- before re-basing onto the new stream (see
3415:    * ChatCodeBase.prior), and ignore stray events only for generations fully left behind.
3416:    * Subscriptions replay each chat's not-yet-materialized changes, so newly-joined clients can
3417:    * reconstruct uncommitted state without a separate fetch; changes a `changes` message has since
3418:    * absorbed are dropped via the message's `watermark` instead (there is no separate "cleared"
3419:    * event).

3422:    * CodeChangeSubmission's clientId and seq), so the submitting client recognizes its own change
3423:    * -- in the live feed and in subscribe-replay alike, without depending on ack/broadcast
3424:    * ordering -- and drops its in-flight buffer instead of re-applying. The echo is informational
3425:    * only; server-authored changes (agent edits, mainline merges) omit it.
3426:    */
3427:   changeApplied(chatId: number, generation: number, revision: number, author: AiChatAuthorInfo,
3428:                 change: CodeChange, submission?: {clientId: string, seq: number}): void;

3430:   /** Delivers one provisional streaming event. Clients may ignore event types they don't support. */
3431:   stream(chatId: number, event: AiChatStreamEvent): void;
3432: }

1: // The operational-transform representation of uncommitted code changes.
2: //
3: // A chat's uncommitted state is a sequence of `CodeChange`s applied on top of committed gadget
4: // code (see ChatCodeBase in the API): every producer -- human keystrokes, agent tool edits,
5: // update-from-mainline merges -- expresses its change against the chat content as of some
6: // revision, and the server serializes them into one revisioned stream per chat. A change
7: // carries no base content, only "a change relative to revision N", which is what lets it
8: // compose with git-backed storage (the base is always some commit's tree plus earlier changes).
9: //
10: // This module is the single owner of the code-change invariants: the wire types, application,
11: // composition, transformation, diffing, the ingestion validation, and the priority convention
12: // all live here and nowhere else. The text-OT core is `@codemirror/state`'s ChangeSet (the
13: // substrate of @codemirror/collab), and change generation uses `fast-diff`; both are private to
14: // this module -- not because they might be swapped out, but so the invariants stay in one
15: // place. The wire carries our own plain-JSON types (structurally ChangeSet's compact JSON
16: // form), keeping the RPC contract self-describing.
17: //
18: // Priority convention (fixed here, used identically on both sides of the wire): for two changes
19: // made concurrently against the same revision, *the change the server ordered earlier comes
20: // first* -- its inserts precede the later change's at equal positions. This is exactly
21: // ChangeSet's documented transform law: `A.compose(B.map(A))` and `B.compose(A.map(B, true))`
22: // produce the same document. `transformCodeChange(a, b)` bakes the pairing in; nothing else may
23: // call the underlying `map`.
24: //
25: // Trust boundary: changes from clients are validated in two stages, and the stages must stay in
26: // this order. `validateCodeChangeSchema` runs *before* any transform -- transformation is
27: // structural and must only ever see well-formed changes -- while `validateCodeChangeContent`
28: // runs *after* transforming the change to the server's current revision, because lengths and
29: // boundaries are only meaningful against the content the change will actually apply to.
30: //
31: // Both stages take a `CodeChange`, and that parameter type is a precondition rather than a
32: // hope: the declared shape is established before they run, by capnweb-validate's generated
33: // validator at the RPC edge (Overseer.submitCodeChange) and by the compiler for the one
34: // in-process producer (the agent's AgentHooks.commitAgentStep, whose changes this module
35: // itself builds). So neither stage re-checks that a value is an object, an array, a pair, or a
36: // string; they check the invariants a TypeScript type cannot express -- canonical gadget keys,
37: // path rules, size caps, integer section lengths, and the one variant rule the wire validator's
38: // first-match union misses (see validateFileChangeSchema).
39: //
40: // Validation's resource-exhaustion goal is deliberately modest: reject anything the caps rule
41: // out in at most one linear pass over input the RPC layer already parsed (with cheap early
42: // exits where they fall out naturally), and no more. Change producers hold edit rights, and a
43: // user who can edit the workspace can do far worse than burn the workspace server's CPU; the
44: // isolate memory limit bounds the blast radius. The size caps exist first for correctness --
45: // composed changes get stored and travel in RPC messages, both of which have hard size limits
46: // of their own -- not as a DoS defense, so don't grow this file chasing sub-linear rejection of
47: // every hostile shape.

53: // Wire types
54: 
55: /**
56:  * A text edit: ChangeSet's compact JSON form. A `TextChange` is a sequence of sections covering
57:  * the *entire* original text -- a bare number retains that many UTF-16 code units, and
58:  * `[deletedLength, ...insertedLines]` replaces `deletedLength` units with the given lines
59:  * (joined by "\n"; a one-element array is a pure deletion). Because sections tile the whole
60:  * text, the change carries its exact before- and after-lengths by construction.
61:  *
62:  * Example: `[2, [2, "😀"], 3]` keeps 2 units, replaces the next 2 with "😀", and keeps the
63:  * final 3 -- valid only against a text of exactly 7 UTF-16 code units.
64:  */

66: 
67: /**

69:  * the three variants applies:

71:  *   doesn't match the change's before-length);

73:  *   including absent;

75:  *   which keeps `remove` composable and transformable without knowing the base.

163:  * subject to its 2MB value cap. V8 writes each string raw (Latin-1 at one byte per UTF-16
164:  * code unit, or UTF-16 at two) plus small structure headers, so two bytes per code unit of
165:  * every string -- gadget keys, paths, `set` text, inserted lines -- plus a fixed share per
166:  * structural node never undercounts; the estimate reads only string lengths, costing O(nodes)
167:  * independent of text size, and is immune to the escape-sequence and multi-byte inflation a
168:  * JSON-text measure would suffer. Callers use it to keep *compositions* of changes inside
169:  * one storable record; `MAX_CODE_CHANGE_SIZE` separately bounds a single change with its own
170:  * unit-weighted measure at validation time.
171:  */
172: export function codeChangeSerializedSize(change: CodeChange): number {
173:   let bytes = SERIALIZED_ENTRY_OVERHEAD;  // the change object's own framing
174:   for (let [gadgetKey, entries] of Object.entries(change)) {
175:     bytes += SERIALIZED_ENTRY_OVERHEAD + 2 * gadgetKey.length;
176:     for (let [path, fileChange] of entries) {
177:       bytes += SERIALIZED_ENTRY_OVERHEAD + 2 * path.length;
178:       if ("set" in fileChange) {
179:         bytes += 2 * fileChange.set.length;
180:       } else if ("edit" in fileChange) {
181:         for (let section of fileChange.edit) {
182:           bytes += SERIALIZED_SECTION_OVERHEAD;
183:           if (typeof section !== "number") {
184:             for (let part of section) {
185:               if (typeof part === "string") bytes += SERIALIZED_LINE_OVERHEAD + 2 * part.length;
186:             }
187:           }
188:         }
189:       }
190:     }
191:   }
192:   return bytes;
193: }
194: 
195: // =======================================================================================
196: // Internal helpers
197: 
198: // Parses a (schema-valid) TextChange into a ChangeSet. fromJSON also throws on malformed input,
199: // making every consumer of an unvalidated change fail closed.
200: function toChangeSet(change: TextChange): ChangeSet {
201:   return ChangeSet.fromJSON(change);
202: }
203: 
204: // Text round-trips all line-separator exotica losslessly: only "\n" is treated as a line
205: // boundary, so "\r", "\r\n", "\u2028", "\u2029", and NUL stay inside their lines.
206: function applyTextChange(text: string, change: TextChange): string {
207:   return toChangeSet(change).apply(Text.of(text.split("\n"))).toString();
208: }
209: 
210: // Iterates a CodeChange's gadget entries as numeric ids. Assumes canonical keys
211: // (schema-validated or produced by this module).
212: function gadgetEntries(change: CodeChange): [number, [string, FileChange][]][] {
213:   return Object.entries(change).map(([key, value]) => [Number(key), value]);
214: }
215: 
216: // Builds a CodeChange with deterministic order (gadgets numeric ascending, entries by path),
217: // dropping empty gadget entries. Determinism matters because changes are stored and compared
218: // (e.g. the migration's conversion-determinism guarantee).
219: function makeCodeChange(gadgets: Map<number, Map<string, FileChange>>): CodeChange {
220:   let change: CodeChange = {};
221:   for (let gadgetId of [...gadgets.keys()].toSorted((x, y) => x - y)) {
222:     let files = gadgets.get(gadgetId)!;
223:     if (files.size === 0) continue;
224:     change[gadgetId] = [...files.keys()].toSorted().map(path => [path, files.get(path)!]);
225:   }
226:   return change;
227: }
228: 
229: // Pairs up two CodeChanges' file entries: yields (gadgetId, path, a's FileChange | undefined,
230: // b's FileChange | undefined) over the union of paths.
231: function* pairedFileChanges(a: CodeChange, b: CodeChange):
232:     Generator<[number, string, FileChange | undefined, FileChange | undefined]> {
233:   let toMaps = (change: CodeChange) => new Map(
234:       gadgetEntries(change).map(([id, entries]) => [id, new Map(entries)]));
235:   let aGadgets = toMaps(a);
236:   let bGadgets = toMaps(b);
237:   for (let gadgetId of new Set([...aGadgets.keys(), ...bGadgets.keys()])) {
238:     let aFiles = aGadgets.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, FileChange>();
239:     let bFiles = bGadgets.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, FileChange>();
240:     for (let path of new Set([...aFiles.keys(), ...bFiles.keys()])) {
241:       yield [gadgetId, path, aFiles.get(path), bFiles.get(path)];
242:     }
243:   }
244: }
245: 
246: // =======================================================================================
247: // Application
248: 
249: /**
250:  * Applies `change` to `content`, returning the resulting content. The input is not modified; the
251:  * result shares the file maps of untouched gadgets with it (treat both as immutable). A gadget
252:  * entry is created for any gadget the change touches. Throws if the change doesn't fit the
253:  * content (an `edit` of an absent file or of a file whose length doesn't match) -- ingestion
254:  * paths must have validated the change first, so a throw here indicates a bug.
255:  */
256: export function applyCodeChange(content: CodeContent, change: CodeChange): CodeContent {
257:   let result = new Map(content);
258:   for (let [gadgetId, fileChanges] of gadgetEntries(change)) {
259:     let files = new Map(result.get(gadgetId));
260:     result.set(gadgetId, files);
261:     for (let [path, fileChange] of fileChanges) {
262:       if ("set" in fileChange) {
263:         files.set(path, fileChange.set);
264:       } else if ("remove" in fileChange) {
265:         files.delete(path);
266:       } else {
267:         let existing = files.get(path);
268:         if (existing === undefined) {
269:           throw new Error(`edit of absent file: gadget ${gadgetId} ${path}`);
270:         }
271:         files.set(path, applyTextChange(existing, fileChange.edit));
272:       }
273:     }
274:   }
275:   return result;
276: }
277: 
278: // =======================================================================================
279: // Composition
280: 
281: /**
282:  * Composes two sequential changes into one with the same effect: `b` must apply to the content
283:  * produced by `a`, and `applyCodeChange(c, composeCodeChange(a, b))` equals
284:  * `applyCodeChange(applyCodeChange(c, a), b)`. Throws on changes that cannot be sequential (an
285:  * `edit` after a `remove`, or edits whose lengths don't chain) -- like `applyCodeChange`, a
286:  * throw indicates a bug in the caller, not bad client input.
287:  */
288: export function composeCodeChange(a: CodeChange, b: CodeChange): CodeChange {
289:   let gadgets = new Map<number, Map<string, FileChange>>();
290:   for (let [gadgetId, path, aChange, bChange] of pairedFileChanges(a, b)) {
291:     let files = gadgets.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, FileChange>();
292:     gadgets.set(gadgetId, files);
293:     files.set(path, composeFileChange(gadgetId, path, aChange, bChange));
294:   }
295:   return makeCodeChange(gadgets);
296: }
297: 
298: function composeFileChange(
299:     gadgetId: number, path: string, a: FileChange | undefined, b: FileChange | undefined)
300:     : FileChange {
301:   if (a === undefined) return b!;
302:   if (b === undefined) return a;
303:   // b is later: its `set` or `remove` wholesale-supersedes whatever a did.
304:   if ("set" in b || "remove" in b) return b;
305:   // b is an edit of a's result.
306:   if ("set" in a) return { set: applyTextChange(a.set, b.edit) };
307:   if ("remove" in a) {
308:     throw new Error(`cannot compose edit after remove: gadget ${gadgetId} ${path}`);
309:   }
310:   return { edit: toChangeSet(a.edit).compose(toChangeSet(b.edit)).toJSON() };
311: }
312: 
313: // =======================================================================================
314: // Transformation
315: 
316: /**
317:  * The result of `transformCodeChange(a, b)`: each input change rebased to apply after the other,
318:  * under the fixed priority pairing. `a` is the original `a` transformed to apply after the
319:  * original `b`; `b` is the original `b` transformed to apply after the original `a`. Applying
320:  * either pairing to the same base -- original `a` then this `b`, or original `b` then this `a`
321:  * -- produces identical content.
322:  */
323: export interface TransformedCodeChanges {
324:   /** The earlier change, rebased to apply after the original `b`. Retains its priority. */
325:   a: CodeChange;
326: 
327:   /** The later change, rebased to apply after the original `a`. */
328:   b: CodeChange;
329: }
330: 
331: /**
332:  * Transforms two concurrent changes (both made against the same content) across each other. `a`
333:  * is the side the server ordered *earlier*, which fixes the priority convention: at equal
334:  * positions, `a`'s inserts precede `b`'s.
335:  *
336:  * Both sides of the wire use this one function. The server rebases an incoming change over the
337:  * changes already accepted since the change's claimed revision (each accepted change is `a`, the
338:  * incoming change is `b`); a client holding unacknowledged local edits rebases them over each
339:  * incoming broadcast change (the broadcast change is `a` -- the server accepted it first -- and
340:  * the client updates its display with the transformed `a` while keeping the transformed `b` as
341:  * its new pending change).
342:  *
343:  * Per-path rules (`set` and `remove` behave alike, so these also cover delete-vs-edit and
344:  * create-vs-create):
345:  * - edit vs edit: delegated to the text OT core under the documented pairing;
346:  * - `set`/`remove` vs an opposing `edit`: the `set`/`remove` survives unchanged and the `edit`
347:  *   is dropped, regardless of order -- its base was wholesale-replaced, so there is nothing
348:  *   meaningful to rebase it onto;
349:  * - `set`/`remove` vs `set`/`remove`: last-writer-wins by server order -- `b` survives, `a` is
350:  *   dropped from the rebased result (it must not clobber `b` when applied after it).
351:  */
352: export function transformCodeChange(a: CodeChange, b: CodeChange): TransformedCodeChanges {
353:   let aGadgets = new Map<number, Map<string, FileChange>>();
354:   let bGadgets = new Map<number, Map<string, FileChange>>();
355:   for (let [gadgetId, path, aChange, bChange] of pairedFileChanges(a, b)) {
356:     let aFiles = aGadgets.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, FileChange>();
357:     aGadgets.set(gadgetId, aFiles);
358:     let bFiles = bGadgets.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, FileChange>();
359:     bGadgets.set(gadgetId, bFiles);
360: 
361:     if (aChange === undefined) {
362:       bFiles.set(path, bChange!);
363:     } else if (bChange === undefined) {
364:       aFiles.set(path, aChange);
365:     } else if ("edit" in aChange && "edit" in bChange) {
366:       let aSet = toChangeSet(aChange.edit);
367:       let bSet = toChangeSet(bChange.edit);
368:       aFiles.set(path, { edit: aSet.map(bSet, true).toJSON() });
369:       bFiles.set(path, { edit: bSet.map(aSet).toJSON() });
370:     } else if ("edit" in aChange) {
371:       // b's set/remove supersedes a's edit.
372:       bFiles.set(path, bChange);
373:     } else if ("edit" in bChange) {
374:       // a's set/remove wholesale-replaced b's base; b's edit is dropped.
375:       aFiles.set(path, aChange);
376:     } else {
377:       // Both set/remove: last-writer-wins by server order.
378:       bFiles.set(path, bChange);
379:     }
380:   }
381:   return { a: makeCodeChange(aGadgets), b: makeCodeChange(bGadgets) };
382: }
383: 
384: // =======================================================================================
385: // Diffing
386: 
387: /**
388:  * Computes the change that turns `before` into `after`:
389:  * `applyCodeChange(before, diffFiles(before, after))` equals `after`. Unchanged files contribute
390:  * nothing; added files become `set`, removed files `remove`, and changed files a minimal
391:  * character-level `edit` whose boundaries never split a UTF-16 surrogate pair. The result is
392:  * deterministic (same inputs, same change, same key and entry order), which the migration's
393:  * conversion messages rely on. Note a gadget with no files diffs identically to an absent
394:  * gadget: a code change carries only file changes, so gadget existence is not represented.
395:  */
396: export function diffFiles(before: CodeContent, after: CodeContent): CodeChange {
397:   let gadgets = new Map<number, Map<string, FileChange>>();
398:   for (let gadgetId of new Set([...before.keys(), ...after.keys()])) {
399:     let beforeFiles = before.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, string>();
400:     let afterFiles = after.get(gadgetId) ?? new Map<string, string>();
401:     let files = new Map<string, FileChange>();
402:     for (let path of new Set([...beforeFiles.keys(), ...afterFiles.keys()])) {
403:       let beforeText = beforeFiles.get(path);
404:       let afterText = afterFiles.get(path);
405:       if (beforeText === afterText) continue;
406:       if (afterText === undefined) {
407:         files.set(path, { remove: true });
408:       } else if (beforeText === undefined) {
409:         files.set(path, { set: afterText });
410:       } else {
411:         files.set(path, { edit: diffTextChange(beforeText, afterText) });
412:       }
413:     }
414:     gadgets.set(gadgetId, files);
415:   }
416:   return makeCodeChange(gadgets);
417: }
418: 
419: // Folds fast-diff's edit script ([kind, text] runs over the whole strings) into ChangeSet
420: // change specs in original coordinates, merging each adjacent delete/insert run into a single
421: // replacement. fast-diff never splits surrogate pairs (verified by fuzz tests), so the
422: // resulting boundaries always pass validateCodeChangeContent.
423: function diffTextChange(before: string, after: string): TextChange {
424:   let specs: { from: number, to: number, insert?: string }[] = [];
425:   let diffs = fastDiff(before, after);
426:   let pos = 0;
427:   for (let i = 0; i < diffs.length; i++) {
428:     let [kind, text] = diffs[i];
429:     if (kind === fastDiff.EQUAL) {
430:       pos += text.length;
431:       continue;
432:     }
433:     // Pair a delete with an immediately following insert (or vice versa) as one replacement.
434:     let deleted = kind === fastDiff.DELETE ? text : "";
435:     let inserted = kind === fastDiff.INSERT ? text : "";
436:     let next = diffs[i + 1];
437:     if (next !== undefined && next[0] !== fastDiff.EQUAL && next[0] !== kind) {
438:       if (next[0] === fastDiff.DELETE) deleted = next[1];
439:       else inserted = next[1];
440:       i++;
441:     }
442:     specs.push({ from: pos, to: pos + deleted.length, insert: inserted });
443:     pos += deleted.length;
444:   }
445:   // The explicit "\n" line separator matters: ChangeSet.of's default splits inserted strings on
446:   // /\r\n?|\n/ and Text rejoins lines with "\n", which would corrupt content containing bare
447:   // "\r". Only "\n" is a line boundary here, matching splitLines' invariants in git-store.
448:   return ChangeSet.of(specs, before.length, "\n").toJSON();
449: }
450: 
451: /**
452:  * Builds the TextChange that replaces `replaced` -- the document's exact text at
453:  * `[from, from + replaced.length)` -- with `insert`, in a document of length `docLength`. The
454:  * producer-side alternative to diffing when the replaced span is already known (editFile matched
455:  * it): no diff is run. A match is often padded with unchanged context to disambiguate it, so the
456:  * common prefix and suffix of `replaced` and `insert` are trimmed -- never splitting a UTF-16
457:  * surrogate pair -- and the change reports only the text that actually changed. Equal `replaced`
458:  * and `insert` yield the identity change; an out-of-range span throws (`ChangeSet.of` rejects it
459:  * at construction).
460:  */
461: export function replaceSpanChange(
462:     docLength: number, from: number, replaced: string, insert: string): TextChange {
463:   let maxTrim = Math.min(replaced.length, insert.length);
464:   let pre = 0;
465:   while (pre < maxTrim && replaced.charCodeAt(pre) === insert.charCodeAt(pre)) pre++;
466:   // Back off a prefix ending on a high surrogate: the boundary could otherwise split a pair in
467:   // the document or in the insert. The prefix chars are equal in both strings, so one
468:   // (conservative) check covers both.
469:   if (pre > 0 && isHighSurrogate(replaced.charCodeAt(pre - 1))) pre--;
470:   let suf = 0;
471:   while (suf < maxTrim - pre && replaced.charCodeAt(replaced.length - 1 - suf) ===
472:       insert.charCodeAt(insert.length - 1 - suf)) {
473:     suf++;
474:   }
475:   // Likewise, back off a retained suffix starting on a low surrogate.
476:   if (suf > 0 && isLowSurrogate(replaced.charCodeAt(replaced.length - suf))) suf--;
477: 
478:   let trimmedInsert = insert.slice(pre, insert.length - suf);
479:   let spec = { from: from + pre, to: from + replaced.length - suf, insert: trimmedInsert };
480:   let specs = spec.from === spec.to && trimmedInsert === "" ? [] : [spec];
481:   // The explicit "\n" line separator: see diffTextChange above.
482:   return ChangeSet.of(specs, docLength, "\n").toJSON();
483: }
484: 
485: // =======================================================================================
486: // Inspection
487: 
488: /** The gadget ids a change touches, ascending. Empty for the identity change. */
489: export function changedGadgets(change: CodeChange): number[] {
490:   return Object.keys(change).map(Number).toSorted((a, b) => a - b);
491: }
492: 
493: // =======================================================================================
494: // Validation (the trust boundary)
495: 
496: /**
497:  * Stage 1 of ingestion validation: the invariants a `CodeChange`'s type cannot express, checked
498:  * *before* any transform (transformation must only ever see schema-valid changes). The declared
499:  * shape is a precondition -- see the trust boundary note at the top of this module -- so this
500:  * verifies canonical decimal gadget keys; non-empty entry lists with non-empty, duplicate-free
501:  * paths; exactly one variant per `FileChange`; that every `edit` parses as a ChangeSet whose
502:  * sections are non-negative integers that each retain, delete, or insert something (do-nothing
503:  * padding is rejected) and whose inserted line strings contain no "\n"; and the size caps:
504:  * `MAX_FILE_TEXT_LENGTH` per produced file, `MAX_FILE_PATH_LENGTH` per path, and
505:  * `MAX_CODE_CHANGE_SIZE` for the change overall. Throws on the first violation.
506:  * Content-dependent checks (lengths, boundaries) are stage 2: `validateCodeChangeContent`.
507:  */
508: export function validateCodeChangeSchema(change: CodeChange): void {
509:   // The size cap is enforced as a running budget, not an after-the-fact sum: an edit's section
510:   // count is pre-checked in O(1) and the budget re-checked as each section's cost accrues, so a
511:   // hostile change is rejected before its sections are walked -- and in particular before
512:   // `ChangeSet.fromJSON` materializes a second copy of an oversized edit.
513:   let remaining = MAX_CODE_CHANGE_SIZE;
514:   for (let [gadgetKey, fileChanges] of Object.entries(change)) {
515:     let gadgetId = Number(gadgetKey);
516:     if (!Number.isSafeInteger(gadgetId) || gadgetId < 0 || String(gadgetId) !== gadgetKey) {
517:       throw new Error(`code change gadget key is not a canonical gadget id: ${gadgetKey}`);
518:     }
519:     if (fileChanges.length === 0) {
520:       throw new Error(`code change gadget entry is empty: gadget ${gadgetKey}`);
521:     }
522:     let seen = new Set<string>();
523:     for (let [path, fileChange] of fileChanges) {
524:       if (path === "") throw new Error(`code change file path is empty: gadget ${gadgetKey}`);
525:       if (path.length > MAX_FILE_PATH_LENGTH) {
526:         throw new Error(`code change file path is too long: gadget ${gadgetKey}`);
527:       }
528:       if (seen.has(path)) {
529:         throw new Error(`code change has a duplicate file entry: gadget ${gadgetKey} ${path}`);
530:       }
531:       seen.add(path);
532:       remaining -= FILE_ENTRY_SIZE_OVERHEAD + path.length;
533:       if (remaining < 0) throw new Error("code change is too large");
534:       remaining -= validateFileChangeSchema(`gadget ${gadgetKey} ${path}`, fileChange, remaining);
535:     }
536:   }
537: }
538: 
539: // Validates one FileChange's schema, returning its payload's share of the change size (see
540: // MAX_CODE_CHANGE_SIZE; always <= budget). Throws "code change is too large" as soon as the
541: // running cost exceeds `budget`, so an oversized payload is rejected without being fully walked.
542: function validateFileChangeSchema(where: string, fileChange: FileChange, budget: number): number {
543:   // Exactly one variant. This one is not the wire validator's to make: its union is first-match
544:   // and extra properties are allowed, so `{set, remove}` reaches us. It must not survive --
545:   // `applyCodeChange` tests `set` before `edit` while `transformCodeChange` tests `edit` first,
546:   // so a two-variant FileChange would be read differently by two replicas and diverge them.
547:   let keys = Object.keys(fileChange);
548:   if (keys.length !== 1 || !["edit", "set", "remove"].includes(keys[0])) {
549:     throw new Error(`file change must have exactly one of edit/set/remove: ${where}`);
550:   }
551:   if ("set" in fileChange) {
552:     if (fileChange.set.length > MAX_FILE_TEXT_LENGTH) {
553:       throw new Error(`file is too large: ${where}`);
554:     }
555:     if (fileChange.set.length > budget) throw new Error("code change is too large");
556:     return fileChange.set.length;
557:   }
558:   if ("remove" in fileChange) return 0;
559:   // ChangeSet.fromJSON is not strict enough on its own -- it accepts negative and non-integer
560:   // section lengths, sections that neither retain, delete, nor insert (free padding that would
561:   // evade the size caps), and inserted "line" strings containing "\n" (which desynchronize the
562:   // resulting document's line metadata from its text) -- so check sections ourselves first;
563:   // fromJSON then rejects the remaining malformed shapes, on input the budget has bounded.
564:   // O(1) budget pre-check on the section count alone, before any section is even looked at.
565:   let cost = fileChange.edit.length * EDIT_SECTION_SIZE_WEIGHT;
566:   if (cost > budget) throw new Error("code change is too large");
567:   for (let section of fileChange.edit) {
568:     if (Array.isArray(section)) {
569:       if (!Number.isSafeInteger(section[0]) || section[0] < 0) {
570:         throw new Error(`file change edit has an invalid section length: ${where}`);
571:       }
572:       // The inserted text's length: the lines' lengths plus the "\n" joining them. The
573:       // separator count is known before the lines are walked, so a section padded with empty
574:       // lines is rejected here in O(1) rather than after the walk.
575:       let insertedHere = section.length >= 2 ? section.length - 2 : 0;
576:       if (cost + insertedHere > budget) throw new Error("code change is too large");
577:       for (let i = 1; i < section.length; i++) {
578:         // A numeric index into `[number, ...string[]]` types as `string | number` because it
579:         // spans every element; every element past the first is a line.
580:         let line = section[i] as string;
581:         if (line.includes("\n")) {
582:           throw new Error(`file change edit inserted line contains a newline: ${where}`);
583:         }
584:         insertedHere += line.length;
585:       }
586:       if (section[0] === 0 && insertedHere === 0) {
587:         throw new Error(`file change edit has a do-nothing section: ${where}`);
588:       }
589:       cost += insertedHere;
590:       if (cost > budget) throw new Error("code change is too large");
591:     } else {
592:       if (!Number.isSafeInteger(section) || section < 0) {
593:         throw new Error(`file change edit has an invalid section length: ${where}`);
594:       }
595:       if (section === 0) throw new Error(`file change edit has a do-nothing section: ${where}`);
596:     }
597:   }
598:   let changes: ChangeSet;
599:   try {
600:     changes = toChangeSet(fileChange.edit);
601:   } catch (e) {
602:     throw new Error(`file change edit is malformed: ${where}: ${e}`, { cause: e });
603:   }
604:   if (changes.newLength > MAX_FILE_TEXT_LENGTH) throw new Error(`file is too large: ${where}`);
605:   return cost;
606: }
607: 
608: /**
609:  * Stage 2 of ingestion validation: the change against the content it will actually apply to,
610:  * checked *after* transforming it to the server's current revision (and only on schema-valid
611:  * changes -- run `validateCodeChangeSchema` first). Verifies each `edit` targets an existing file
612:  * of exactly the change's before-length, that every change boundary lands on a code-point
613:  * boundary of that file, and that no inserted or `set` text contains a lone UTF-16 surrogate.
614:  * The surrogate rules are what keep replicas byte-identical: changes travel as UTF-8 (where a
615:  * lone surrogate decodes as U+FFFD), so a mid-pair boundary or a lone surrogate would make remote
616:  * replicas disagree with the sender. Throws on the first violation.
617:  */
618: export function validateCodeChangeContent(change: CodeChange, content: CodeContent): void {
619:   for (let [gadgetId, fileChanges] of gadgetEntries(change)) {
620:     for (let [path, fileChange] of fileChanges) {
621:       let where = `gadget ${gadgetId} ${path}`;
622:       if ("set" in fileChange) {
623:         if (hasLoneSurrogate(fileChange.set)) {
624:           throw new Error(`file change set contains a lone surrogate: ${where}`);
625:         }
626:       } else if ("edit" in fileChange) {
627:         let text = content.get(gadgetId)?.get(path);

648: // Whether position `pos` in `text` is a code-point boundary, i.e. does not fall between the
649: // halves of a surrogate pair.
650: function isCodePointBoundary(text: string, pos: number): boolean {
651:   if (pos <= 0 || pos >= text.length) return true;
652:   return !(isHighSurrogate(text.charCodeAt(pos - 1)) && isLowSurrogate(text.charCodeAt(pos)));

655: function isHighSurrogate(code: number): boolean {
656:   return code >= 0xd800 && code < 0xdc00;

659: function isLowSurrogate(code: number): boolean {
660:   return code >= 0xdc00 && code < 0xe000;
661: }

664: function hasLoneSurrogate(text: string): boolean {
665:   for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
666:     let code = text.charCodeAt(i);
667:     if (isHighSurrogate(code)) {
668:       if (i + 1 >= text.length || !isLowSurrogate(text.charCodeAt(i + 1))) return true;
669:       i++;  // Skip the low half of a well-formed pair.
670:     } else if (isLowSurrogate(code)) {
671:       return true;
672:     }
673:   }

525: export interface GatekeeperConnectCallback extends WorkerEntrypoint {

527:    * Indicates the connection completed successfully.

529:    * `expiresAt`, if provided, indicates when the credentials are expected to stop being

542:    * Called when the gatekeeper discovers that credentials have expired or been revoked (e.g., a

558: /**
559:  * RPC interface to an Adapter. This is a privileged interface exposed to the Gadget Workshop UI
560:  * itself, not to Gadgets nor AI agents.
561:  *
562:  * The Adapter is already specialized for a particular human user of the Gadget Workshop. The
563:  * Adapter capability itself represents permission to access all of the user's data that is
564:  * available through it, so needs to be guarded carefully. Hence, only the Workshop itself should
565:  * ever have direct access to an Adapter object.
566:  */

568:   /** Get display info for an account, suitable for display to a user. */

571:   /**
572:    * Typically returns the same as GatekeeperVendor.getSupportedResources(), though an

579:    * Get a Durable Object class that can implement a gatekeeper for the given resource. This class
580:    * can be used to instantiate a Facet which implements the Gatekeeper interface.
581:    *

592:     resource: SupportedResource;
593:   }>;

595:   /**
596:    * Get the UI used to choose a specific resource.
597:    * `resourceUrlPattern` is the `urlPattern` associated with the supported resource.

600:     resourceUrlPattern: string,
601:   ): Promise<ResourceConfiguratorFrame>;
602: 
603:   /**
604:    * Revoke this account connection. The GatekeeperUser, and all Gatekeepers created through it,

606:    */
607:   revoke(): Promise<void>;
608: 
609:   /**
610:    * Start the flow to refresh/replace credentials on this account. Returns the URL for the user

612:    * GatekeeperConnectCallback (provided during the original connectAccount() flow) will be

614:    * created through it continue to work with the new credentials.

616:    * SECURITY: As with connectAccount(), the returned URL must include a cryptographic nonce to
617:    * prevent replay attacks.
618:    */

621:   /**
622:    * For vendors that advertise `providesAuth`, returns the account's email address for use as the

627:    */
628:   getAuthenticatedEmail(): Promise<string | null>;
629: 
630:   /** Get a `GatekeeperUserVerifier` representing this user. */
631:   getVerifier(): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>>;
632: 
633:   /**
634:    * Ensure the authorization for the listed grantable resource types (by `urlPattern`) is granted
635:    * on this account, expanding the grant if needed.

637:    * Returns the URL for the user to visit to authorize them, or no URL if nothing was needed.
638:    * Gatekeepers with no grantable resource types should return no URL.
639:    *
640:    * SECURITY: As with connectAccount(), any returned URL must include a cryptographic nonce.
641:    */
642:   ensureResources(resourceUrlPatterns: string[]): Promise<{url?: string}>;
643: 
644:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
645:   // Singleton / management-UI capabilities. Present only on accounts created by
646:   // GatekeeperVendor.createAccount() whose describe() sets AccountDescription.singleton and/or

651:    * Get a Durable Object class implementing the account's agent singleton, for accounts whose
652:    * describe() sets AccountDescription.singleton. The Workshop installs this gatekeeper into the

654:    * its session to the agent as an unnamed capsule. Because it is a normal Gatekeeper, the session

659:    * The returned class is imbued (via `ctx.props`) with whatever the account needs to serve the

662:   getSingletonGatekeeperClass?(): Promise<DurableObjectClass<Gatekeeper<any>>>;
663: 
664:   /**
665:    * The account's full-page management UI (iframe HTML + ui capability). `context.isAdmin` is passed
666:    * fresh per open (not baked into the account) so admin-gated features reflect current status.
667:    */
668:   startAppUi?(context: AppUiContext): Promise<GatekeeperUiFrame>;
669: 
670:   // TODO:
671:   // - Query whether account has scope to access a particular URL.
672: }

674: /**
675:  * Opaque object representing the capability to verify whether a particular user is able to access
676:  * a particular Gatekeeper. Minted by `GatekeeperUser`, and then passed to
677:  * `Gatekeeper.addObserver()` and possibly other future interfaces.
678:  *
679:  * At present, this interface has no methods, because it is merely meant to be passed back to the
680:  * Gatekeeper that created it.
681:  *
682:  * IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: As of this writing, there is no runtime-supported way to "unwrap" a
683:  * `Fetcher` passed back to its implementer in order to extract the underlying `props`. This will
684:  * be added eventually. For now, we recommend that the `GatekeeperUserVerifier` implement a public
685:  * but non-standard method which the same gatekeeper's `addObserver()` implementations can call.
686:  * The overseer promises only to pass a `GatekeeperUserVerifier` object back to the same gatekeeper
687:  * that created it, so addObserver() can then call that non-standard method and trust the results.
688:  */
689: export interface GatekeeperUserVerifier extends WorkerEntrypoint {}
